title: "Missing data imputation"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 96

```

Follow-up is rarely complete: a visit happens but one lab is not drawn, or a
biomarker is only measured for some patients. `imputeLongitudinal()` fills in
the missing biomarker values before the longitudinal sub-models are fit, and
`poolLongitudinalSub()` combines the fits to several completions. This
article starts with the question that comes first: **do you need to impute
at all?** Often you do not.

| Step | Function |
|---|---|
| Fill in missing biomarker values (one or several completions) | `imputeLongitudinal()` |
| Fit each completion | `longitudinalSub()` |
| Combine the fits (Rubin's rules) into one, also for prediction | `poolLongitudinalSub()` |

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(BJM)
data(pbc3)
```

## What BJM does without imputation

Without imputation, `longitudinalSub()` fits each biomarker's linear mixed
model by maximum likelihood on every visit at which *that* biomarker was
measured. Under the usual assumption that values are **missing at random**
(whether a value is missing depends only on what is observed), this is
already a valid analysis: the mixed model uses each patient's observed
values, and nothing is gained by filling in the others with values drawn
from the same model.

Only one part of the fit uses complete cases: the joint covariance of the
random effects across biomarkers, `Sigma_fit`, which every prediction uses,
is estimated from the patients with at least one value of *every*
biomarker. A patient who never had some biomarker measured is left out of
it. This is what imputation can recover.

## Do you need to impute? A simulation

To find out, we took the `pbc3` patients with an event, deleted biomarker
values at random, and compared each method's predictions with those of the
fit to the complete data. Each method's fits to the completed data sets were
pooled with `poolLongitudinalSub()` (multiple imputation, 5 completions).
The prediction error is the mean absolute difference, over 245 patients
event-free at year 3, between the predicted 2-year risks and those of the
complete-data fit; averages over 20 random deletions. In the complete data,
the albumin random-intercept variance is 0.072 and the albumin `years`
(event-time) coefficient 0.078.

| Missing | Method | Prediction error | Albumin intercept variance | Albumin `years` coefficient |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 15% of visits miss each biomarker | no imputation | **0.0056** | 0.071 | 0.078 |
| | `"mixed"` | **0.0056** | 0.070 | 0.078 |
| | `"miwae"`, `history = TRUE` | 0.0062 | 0.067 | 0.078 |
| | `"diffusion"`, `history = TRUE` | 0.0077 | 0.062 | 0.076 |
| | `"miwae"` | 0.0165 | 0.051 | 0.077 |
| 30% of patients never had albumin | no imputation | **0.0108** | 0.072 | 0.078 |
| | `"mixed"` | 0.0114 | 0.073 | 0.078 |
| | `"miwae"` | 0.0116 | 0.053 | 0.078 |
| | `"miwae"`, `history = TRUE` | 0.0141 | 0.062 | 0.074 |
| | `"diffusion"`, `history = TRUE` | 0.0157 | 0.060 | 0.067 |
| 50% of patients never had albumin | no imputation | 0.0167 | 0.070 | 0.077 |
| | `"mixed"` | **0.0159** | 0.074 | 0.079 |
| | `"miwae"` | 0.0192 | 0.042 | 0.078 |
| | `"diffusion"`, `history = TRUE` | 0.0227 | 0.047 | 0.061 |
| | `"miwae"`, `history = TRUE` | 0.0235 | 0.052 | 0.073 |

What this shows:

* **With visits missing values at random, do not impute.** No method beat
  the analysis without imputation; the mixed-model imputation tied it.
* **With many patients missing a biomarker entirely**, multiple imputation
  with `method = "mixed"` (the default) helped a little at 50% (closer to
  the complete data in 15 of the 20 deletions), and was about even at 30%
  (closer in 8 of 20).
* **`"mixed"` is the only method that left the model unbiased.** The deep
  generative methods shrank the variation between patients (the albumin
  intercept variance), and with `history = TRUE` they also biased the
  event-time coefficient, the link between the biomarker and the event that
  every BJM prediction rests on.

Imputation is also worth it when values are missing for reasons recorded in
variables that are *not* in the model (auxiliary variables): add them to the
formulas used for imputation, then fit the model without them.

## Imputing with the mixed model

To illustrate, we delete albumin for 30% of the patients:

```{r data}
fixed <- list(serBilir = serBilir ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year,
              albumin  = albumin  ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year)
random <- list(serBilir = ~ year | id, albumin = ~ year | id)
complete <- pbc3[pbc3$status3 == 1, ]

set.seed(1)
never <- sample(unique(complete$id), round(0.3 * length(unique(complete$id))))
whole <- complete
whole$albumin[whole$id %in% never] <- NA
```

`imputeLongitudinal()` takes the same data and formulas as
`longitudinalSub()`, plus the visit-time variable. With the default
`method = "mixed"`, it fits that same multivariate mixed model and draws each
patient's missing values from their distribution given everything observed
for the patient: all visits, and the other biomarkers through `Sigma_fit`.
For each completion the model's parameters are first drawn from their
approximate posterior, so the completions also carry the uncertainty about
the fit. It needs no extra package and takes a second or two.

```{r impute}
imputed <- imputeLongitudinal(whole, fixed, random, time_variable = "year",
                              impute = "multiple", n_imputations = 5, seed = 1)
names(imputed)
```

`data_fit_all_list` holds the five completed data sets, each a list with one
data frame per biomarker, ready for `longitudinalSub()` with the same
formulas. Fit each, and pool the fits:

```{r pool}
fits <- lapply(imputed$data_fit_all_list, function(d) longitudinalSub(d, fixed, random))
pooled <- poolLongitudinalSub(fits)
round(pooled$pooled$albumin, 4)
```

`fmi`, the fraction of missing information, is the share of a coefficient's
variance that is due to the missing values. `pooled$long_fit_all` is a fit
for prediction: the pooled fixed effects, and the averages of the fits'
residual variances and `Sigma_fit`. Compared with the complete-data fit and
the fit without imputation:

```{r compare}
fit_complete <- longitudinalSub(complete, fixed, random)
fit_none <- longitudinalSub(whole, fixed, random)
summarise <- function(f) c(albumin_intercept_var = f$Sigma_fit[3, 3],
                           albumin_years = nlme::fixef(f$lfit[[2]])[["years"]],
                           cor_intercepts = cov2cor(f$Sigma_fit)[1, 3])
round(rbind(complete_data = summarise(fit_complete), no_imputation = summarise(fit_none),
            mixed_imputation = summarise(pooled$long_fit_all)), 3)
```

A single deletion like this one is noisy: here neither fit is clearly closer
to the complete data than the other. The simulation above, which averages
over 20 deletions, is what the advice rests on.

`diagnostics` compares, for each biomarker, the observed values with the
imputed ones (the means of the draws), and with a classical baseline (each
biomarker regressed on the covariates):

```{r diagnostics}
d <- imputed$diagnostics$albumin
round(rbind(mixed = unlist(d$deep_generative), baseline = unlist(d$classical_baseline)), 3)
```

### Predicting with an imputed fit

The pooled fit is used for prediction like any other. Only the data the
models are fit on are imputed; a patient's own history is used as observed,
missing values and all (`predictRisk()` drops a missing value and keeps the
rest of the visit):

```{r predict}
survival_fit <- survivalSub(pbc3[!duplicated(pbc3$id), ], Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex, NULL)
patient <- pbc3[pbc3$id == 2 & pbc3$year <= 5, ]
patient$years <- NA
patient$albumin[2] <- NA
predictRisk(list(patient, patient), pooled$long_fit_all, survival_fit,
            prediction_time = 5, horizon = 2, time_variable = "year",
            survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
```

### One completion or several

`impute = "single"` (the default) returns one completed data set,
`data_fit_all`, each missing value the mean of the `n_imputations` draws. A
model fit to it treats the imputed values as observed: its standard errors
are too small, and its variances, including `Sigma_fit`, are too small the
more is imputed. Prefer `impute = "multiple"` with `poolLongitudinalSub()`
unless very little is missing.

## Deep generative alternatives

`method = "miwae"` (a variational autoencoder for incomplete data; Mattei
and Frellsen, 2019) and `method = "diffusion"` (a conditional diffusion
model as in CSDI; Tashiro et al., 2021) learn the joint distribution of the
biomarkers and covariates with a neural network instead. They complete each
visit from that visit's covariates and observed biomarkers, which is why
they shrink the variation between patients; `history = TRUE` adds a summary
of the patient's other visits to the inputs. They are flexible, but as the
simulation shows, on BJM's longitudinal data they did not do better than the
mixed model, and could bias the model. They need the **torch** package and
its backend (`install.packages("torch")`, then `torch::install_torch()`).

```{r torch-check}
torch_available <- requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(tryCatch(torch::torch_is_installed(), error = function(e) FALSE))
```

```{r deep, eval = torch_available}
imputed_miwae <- imputeLongitudinal(whole, fixed, random, time_variable = "year",
                                    method = "miwae", impute = "multiple", seed = 1)
fits_miwae <- lapply(imputed_miwae$data_fit_all_list, function(d) longitudinalSub(d, fixed, random))
round(summarise(poolLongitudinalSub(fits_miwae)$long_fit_all), 3)
```

## Things to watch for

* **Missing at random.** Every method assumes that whether a value is
  missing depends only on what is observed. A lab skipped because the
  patient was too ill breaks this, and no imputation fixes it.
* **Only biomarkers are imputed.** The covariates of the formulas and the
  visit times must be complete, and the biomarkers continuous.
* **Check on your own data.** Delete some observed values at random, impute
  them, and compare with what was deleted and with the fit without
  imputation, as in the simulation above.
* **Reproducibility.** `seed` fixes the random numbers of the call (and
  torch's, for the deep methods, whose results can still differ slightly
  between computers).

## References

Mattei, P.-A. and Frellsen, J. (2019). MIWAE: Deep generative modelling and
imputation of incomplete data sets. *Proceedings of the 36th International
Conference on Machine Learning*, PMLR 97:4413--4423.

Rubin, D. B. (1987). *Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys*. Wiley.

Tashiro, Y., Song, J., Song, Y. and Ermon, S. (2021). CSDI: Conditional
score-based diffusion models for probabilistic time series imputation.
*Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems*, 34:24804--24816.
